reviews.reason: Both make maximum-change rescaling and final-only division intelligible: A's 'same exponential scale' and B's 'full-row softmax' explain the same invariant. P03 Sec. 3.1.1, Algorithm 1 (steps 9-13), and its correctness paragraph support exact output, saved logsumexp, quadratic arithmetic, and linear auxiliary storage. Their ordering differences do not materially affect the methods function.

A's 'each warp its own query rows' and B's row-specific denominator explain the same row independence and removal of forward reductions. P03 Secs. 3.2-3.3 support both warp and thread-block partitioning; Sec. 3.1.1 supports deferred normalization and logsumexp storage. B's backward-synchronization qualification is accurate, but neither version materially improves the explanation over the other.

Both link unchanged exact attention to reduced normalization work and query-row parallelism, then distinguish kernel gains from smaller training gains. P03 Secs. 3.1-3.3, 4.1, and Table 1 support those relationships and figures. B's 'uniform application-level speedup' is slightly clearer than A's 'full kernel-level acceleration,' but this wording difference is a near tie.

Both explain rescaled accumulators, final normalization, backward recomputation, and query-row ownership accurately (P03 Algorithm 1; Secs. 3.2-3.3). The concluding register-spilling and capacity limits also match Sec. 3.3. B's 'shared-memory traffic' is slightly more precise than A's 'transfers,' but their mechanisms, evidence selection, and overall methods exposition remain equivalent.

A's 'different benefits' and B's 'do not transfer proportionally' correctly distinguish training throughput from kernel speed and memory feasibility. P03 Sec. 4.3, Table 1 supports the larger 8k gains and the unhalved FLOPs convention; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 4 supports PyTorch OOM at 16k with fixed total tokens. B's additional 2.7B comparison is pertinent but not decisive.

B's 'smaller, context-dependent gains' connects the kernel results to an interpretable training comparison (170 to 220 versus 189 to 196), supported by P03 Sec. 4.3, Table 1. A's absolute 225-TFLOPs/s peak is accurate but leaves the training effect less clear. Both correctly distinguish training's execution costs from decoding's KV-cache bottleneck (Secs. 3.2, 4.2).

B explicitly connects 'guesses sequentially' with target verification 'concurrently,' explaining the execution schedule behind the gamma*c cost term. A accurately explains correction but leaves that central scheduling step implicit. P04 Sec. 2.1 and Algorithm 1 support the staged schedule; Secs. 3.1 and 3.3 support both yield and timing formulas. Both preserve the target distribution.

A makes rejection-weighted residual mass explicit; B gives the same exactness argument and additionally connects token yield to walltime. P04 Sec. 2.3 and Algorithm 1 support both prefix-handling accounts; Secs. 3.1, 3.3-3.4 support yield, conditional speedup, and the distinction from arithmetic savings. These are comparably effective methods paragraphs with different, well-supported closing emphases.

A's 'without substituting' and B's 'preserving' both clearly distinguish exact target sampling from draft quality. P04 Secs. 2.1-2.3 and 3.3 support their mechanisms and timing assumptions; Sec. 4.1, Table 2 supports the TPU-v4 setup and all four T5 speedups. B foregrounds spare hardware capacity; A identifies T5X and English-to-German explicitly. Neither advantage is decisive.

A separates distributional correctness from speed assumptions; B makes the extra timing conditions explicit at its close. Both correctly use 'normalized positive part' correction and accepted-prefix retention (P04 Sec. 2.3, Algorithm 1). Their expected-yield and speedup formulas match Secs. 3.1 and 3.3, including i.i.d. acceptance, long generations, and unchanged concurrent target latency. This is a near tie.

A uses the matched-seven-guess greedy comparison; B uses standard-sampling configurations and explicitly notes their differing guess counts. P04 Sec. 4.1, Table 2 supports both routes to the conclusion that acceptance alone is insufficient. Secs. 3.3-3.4 support the cost tradeoff and wasted arithmetic. Their different evidence selections serve their stated results claims equally well.

Both distinguish roughly 1.3-fold training gains from 1.7-3.0-fold kernel gains and interpret the reported 72% using its FLOPs convention (P03 Sec. 4.3, Table 1). Their PyTorch-versus-tiled memory comparison matches Sec. 4.1, Fig. 4. B names the fixed-16k-token setting explicitly; A locates the result in the separate benchmarks. The overall results interpretation is effectively equivalent.

Both explain probability-mass correction, separate exactness from conditional acceleration, and bound the measured gains to batch-one T5 tests. P04 Secs. 2.3, 3.3-3.6, and 4.1, Table 2 support these claims. A's 'improved agreement must compensate for proposal cost' and B's 'tradeoff between agreement and proposal cost' draw the same justified inference. Neither offers a material abstract-level advantage.

Both organize the contribution around independent query rows and distinguish training from KV-cache-limited decoding. P03 Secs. 3.1-3.3 support the mechanisms; Secs. 4.1-4.3 support the kernel, training, and FasterTransformer comparisons. B states the 8k-versus-2k pattern directly, while A concludes with smaller, context-dependent whole-model gains. Both faithfully summarize the same contribution without a decisive difference.

A explains the residual's role in restoring target mass; B more compactly names acceptance and residual resampling while foregrounding the guess-cost tradeoff. Both are supported by P04 Secs. 2.3 and 3.3-3.4. Sec. 4.1, Table 2 supports their matched setup and speedup figures. Their differing mechanism detail and tradeoff emphasis are equally appropriate for an abstract.

Both use the fixed-seven-proposal greedy comparison to show that higher acceptance need not produce lower latency (P04 Sec. 4.1, Table 2). A distinguishes GPT-like/LaMDA acceptance measurements from T5 walltime results, matching Sec. 4.2; B identifies unchanged proposal counts across sampling comparisons. Both selections are pertinent, and both correctly connect rejected work and spare compute to Sec. 3.4.

A's 'does not offset its proposal cost' and B's 'does not by itself offset' interpret the same fixed-length greedy comparison appropriately. P04 Sec. 4.1, Table 2 supports acceptance and speedup figures; Sec. 4.2 confirms that GPT-like/LaMDA tests measured acceptance only. Both explain sampling dependence and rejected computation without extending the demonstrated latency gains beyond T5. Their differences are minor.

Both infer context dependence from the 2k/8k comparisons and distinguish training FLOPs accounting from causally masked kernel accounting (P03 Secs. 4.1, 4.3, Table 1). B's 'not a new memory advantage over FlashAttention' explicitly identifies the memory comparison's scope; A also names PyTorch as the baseline. Both match Fig. 4's 16k OOM result. These are comparably effective results paragraphs.
